'''Gérard Albert Mourou''' ({{IPA|fr|ʒeʁaʁ muʁu|lang}}; born 22 June 1944)<ref name="Lindinger">{{cite news |last=Lindinger |first=Manfred |date=2 October 2018 |title=Eine Zange aus lauter Licht |url=https://www.faz.net/aktuell/wissen/nobelpreise/physik-nobelpreis-2018-praezisionswerkzeuge-aus-laserlicht-15818493.html |work=[[Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung]] |language=de |access-date=6 October 2018}}</ref> is a French scientist and pioneer in the field of [[electrical engineering]] and [[lasers]].  He was awarded a [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 2018, along with [[Donna Strickland]], for the invention of [[chirped pulse amplification]], a technique later used to create ultrashort-pulse, very high-intensity ([[petawatt]]) laser pulses.<ref name=Michigan_Profile>{{cite web |url=http://www.engin.umich.edu/research/cuos/ResearchGroups/HFS/Profiles/Gerard_Mourou.html |title=Gérard Mourou |date=2 October 2018 |publisher=University of Michigan |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080905085848/http://www.engin.umich.edu/research/cuos/ResearchGroups/HFS/Profiles/Gerard_Mourou.html |archive-date=5 September 2008 }}</ref>

In 1994, Mourou and his team at the [[University of Michigan]] discovered that the balance between the self-focusing refraction (see [[Kerr effect]]) and self-attenuating [[diffraction]] by [[ionization]] and rarefaction of a laser beam of terawatt intensities in the atmosphere creates "filaments" that act as [[waveguide]]s for the beam, thus preventing divergence.

==Career==
Mourou was born on 22 June 1944 in [[Albertville]], France.<ref name="Nobel">{{cite web |date=5 October 2018 |title=Gérard Mourou – Facts – 2018 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/mourou/facts/ |work=NobelPrize.org |publisher=Nobel Media AB |access-date=5 October 2018}}</ref> Mourou obtained a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] degree from [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]] in 1973. He then moved to the United States, spending a year as a postdoctoral student at the [[University of California, San Diego|University of California San Diego]]. He later became a professor at the [[University of Rochester]] in 1977, where he and his then student [[Donna Strickland]] produced their Nobel prize-winning work in the [[Laboratory for Laser Energetics]] at the university in the 1980s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rochester.edu/newscenter/rochesters-breakthrough-in-laser-science-earns-nobel-prize-340302/ |title=Rochester breakthrough in laser science earns Nobel Prize |date=2 October 2018 |website=University of Rochester |access-date=4 October 2018}}</ref> The pair co-invented [[chirped pulse amplification]], a "method of generating high-intensity, ultra-short optical pulses".<ref name="bbc2">{{cite news |last1=Murphy |first1=Jessica |date=2 October 2018 |title=Donna Strickland: The 'laser jock' Nobel prize winner |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-45722890 |access-date=2 October 2018 |work=BBC News}}</ref> Strickland's doctoral thesis was on "development of an ultra-bright laser and an application to multi-photon ionization".<ref name="Thesis">{{cite thesis |last=Strickland |first=Donna Theo |title=Development of an ultra-bright laser and an application to multi-photon ionization |date=1988 |access-date=6 October 2018 |type=PhD |publisher=University of Rochester |url=http://www.lle.rochester.edu/media/publications/documents/theses/Strickland.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130707150743/http://www.lle.rochester.edu/media/publications/documents/theses/Strickland.pdf |archive-date=7 July 2013 |author-link=Donna Strickland |url-status=live}}</ref> 

Mourou joined the [[University of Michigan]] in 1988, where he became the founding director of the Center for Ultrafast Optical Science in 1990<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 20, 2017 |author=Catharine June |title=CUOS: Pushing the limits of optical science |url=https://ece.engin.umich.edu/stories/cuos-pushing-the-limits-of-optical-science/ |access-date=2026-02-19 |website=Electrical and Computer Engineering |language=en-US}}</ref> or 1991.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=U-M professor emeritus shares 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics |website=The University Record |url=https://record.umich.edu/articles/u-m-professor-emeritus-shares-2018-nobel-prize-physics/ |access-date=2026-02-18}}</ref> He subsequently returned to France as a professor at the [[École Polytechnique|École polytechnique]] to direct the Laboratoire d'optique appliquée at [[ENSTA]] from 2005 to 2009 and develop the [[Extreme Light Infrastructure|Extreme Light Infrastructure project]] from 2007 on.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-10-27 |title=CV - Gérard Mourou |url=https://mediatheque.lindau-nobel.org/laureates/morou/cv |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251109130519/https://mediatheque.lindau-nobel.org/laureates/morou/cv |archive-date=2025-11-09 |access-date=2026-02-18 |work=Lindau Nobel Mediatheque |language=en-US}}</ref> 

In October 2024, he was appointed as a Chair Professor at Peking University.<ref>{{Cite web | title=French Nobel-Winning Laser Scientist Joins China’s Top Institute; Could Play Key Role To Meet Beijing's Ambitions | url=https://www.eurasiantimes.com/chinas-growing-scientific-appeal-nobel/ | access-date=2026-07-07 | website=www.eurasiantimes.com}}</ref> He is also the A. D. Moore Distinguished University Professor Emeritus at the University of Michigan.<ref name=":0" /> 

=== Nobel Prize ===
[[File:Ecole polytechnique (31183345568).jpg|thumb|262px|Mourou, speaking in 2018 after being awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Physics|Nobel Prize]]]]
On 2 October 2018, Mourou and [[Donna Strickland|Strickland]] were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics, for their joint work on [[chirped pulse amplification]].<ref name="Physics Nobel prize won">{{cite news |title=Physics Nobel prize won by Arthur Ashkin, Gérard Mourou and Donna Strickland |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2018/oct/02/arthur-ashkin-gerard-mourou-and-donna-strickland-win-nobel-physics-prize |first=Ian|last= Sample|author2= Nicola Davis|access-date=2 October 2018 |work=The Guardian |date=2 October 2018}}</ref> They shared half of the Prize, while the other half was awarded to [[Arthur Ashkin]] for his invention of "optical tweezers that grab particles, atoms, viruses and other living cells with their laser beam fingers".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/arthur-ashkin-2-others-win-nobel-physics-prize-for-laser-research/ |title=Arthur Ashkin, 2 others win Nobel Physics Prize for laser research |date=2 October 2018 |website=Times of Israel |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref><ref name="physicsworld.com">{{cite web |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/arthur-ashkin-gerard-mourou-and-donna-strickland-the-nobel-prize-for-physics/ |title=Arthur Ashkin, Gérard Mourou and Donna Strickland win the Nobel Prize for Physics |website= Physics World |first=Hamish |last=Johnston|date=2 October 2018 |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref>

[[File:Gérard Mourou EM1B5793 (46234161551).jpg|thumb|262px|Gérard Mourou during Nobel press conference in [[Stockholm]], December 2018]]

Mourou and Strickland found that stretching a laser out reduced its peak power, which could then be greatly amplified using normal instruments.
It could then be compressed to create the short-lived, highly powerful lasers they were after.<ref name="physicsworld.com" /> The technique, which was described in Strickland's first scientific publication, came to be known as chirped pulse amplification (CPA). They were probably unaware at the time that their tools would make it possible to study natural phenomena in unprecedented ways.<ref name="physicsworld.com" /> CPA could also per definition be used to create a laser pulse that only lasts one attosecond, one-billionth of a billionth of a second. At those timescales, it became possible not only to study chemical reactions, but what happens inside individual atoms.<ref name="physicsworld.com" />

''[[The Guardian]]'' and [[Scientific American]] provided simplified summaries of the work of Strickland and Mourou: it "paved the way for the shortest, most intense laser beams ever created". "The ultrabrief, ultrasharp beams can be used to make extremely precise cuts so their technique is now used in laser machining and enables doctors to perform millions of corrective" [[laser eye surgery|laser eye surgeries]].<ref name="Physics Nobel prize won" /><ref>{{cite web |title='Optical Tweezers' and Tools Used for Laser Eye Surgery Snag Physics Nobel |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/optical-tweezers-and-tools-used-for-laser-eye-surgery-snag-physics-nobel1/ |access-date=2 October 2018 |first=Lee |last=Billings|website=Scientific American |date=2 October 2018}}</ref> Canadian Prime Minister [[Justin Trudeau]] acknowledged the achievements of Mourou and Strickland: "Their innovative work can be found in applications including corrective eye surgery, and is expected to have a significant impact on cancer therapy and other physics research in the future".<ref>[https://pm.gc.ca/eng/news/2018/10/02/statement-prime-minister-donna-strickland-winning-nobel-prize-physics Statement by the Prime Minister on Donna Strickland winning the Nobel Prize in Physics], PMO, 2 October 2018.</ref>

== Controversy ==
At the time he received the Nobel prize, a publicity video filmed in 2010 to represent the [[Extreme Light Infrastructure]] (ELI), went viral. It featured female students swaying around Mourou and losing their lab coats. It was widely criticized, included by the Nobel committee for its representation of women in sciences.<ref name="LeMonde">{{Cite news |last=Morin |first=Hervé |date=2 October 2018 |title=Quand le Nobel Gérard Mourou se mettait en scène dans un clip musical potache |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/sciences/article/2018/10/02/quand-le-nobel-gerard-mourou-se-mettait-en-scene-dans-un-clip-musical-potache_5363583_1650684.html |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=Le Monde |quote=Le laboratoire avait contacté une compagnie de théâtre spécialisée dans les sujets scientifiques..en 2008. C'est à cette occasion que <nowiki>[réalisateur]</nowiki> Mokaddem Djemel a rencontré les chercheurs. De fil en aiguille, l'idée d'une vidéo a germé, utilisant une chanson du spectacle. (The lab contacted a theatre company specializing in scientific subjects..in 2008. It was then that <nowiki>[filmmaker]</nowiki> Mokaddem Djemel met the researchers. Gradually, the idea of a video was born, using a song from the show.)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=14 November 2013 |title=Have you seen ELI3 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k6i7A8Plqb8 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/k6i7A8Plqb8 |archive-date=2021-12-21 |access-date=2 October 2018 |website=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref> Mourou commented it was intended as humoristic, and added: ''"I am not very proud of this video".''<ref>{{Cite news |date=2018-10-02 |title=Quand le Nobel Gérard Mourou se mettait en scène dans un clip musical potache |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/sciences/article/2018/10/02/quand-le-nobel-gerard-mourou-se-mettait-en-scene-dans-un-clip-musical-potache_5363583_1650684.html |access-date=2026-02-18 |language=fr |quote=« Je ne suis pas très fier de cette vidéo, faite pour montrer que les chercheurs peuvent se décontracter »}}</ref>
